title: Career Cosmic Roast
tagline: Your shift has been written in the stars, regrettably.
premise: Three rounds. Each round deals the same ordinary job title to both players. Each writes one sentence of horoscope predicting what will happen during that job's workday. Keep the job recognizable, but let the stars become wildly overconfident. The Judge scores each prophecy, then both players choose which horoscope was written by the rival and which by the House. Then the cosmic verdict arrives.

tests: The card names an ordinary job title a player can recognize.
The horoscope predicts something that could happen during that job's workday.
The prophecy preserves the title's main duty rather than replacing it with fantasy.
The sentence is dramatic, specific, and no more than 160 characters.
The joke gives the job a cosmic problem without making the job itself disappear.

move_constraints.example: Today, your dough rises beautifully, but a jealous wedding cake demands a corner office.
move_constraints.hint: One sentence, under 160 characters. Name the job, predict its day, and let the stars overreact.

rubric.name: believable
rubric.description: Could this plausibly happen during the workday of the named job, even if the horoscope gives it an absurdly grand twist?
rubric.anchors: 0 = unrelated to the job; 1 = barely attached; 2 = possible with a generous horoscope; 3 = clearly belongs to that workday; 4 = so apt it feels professionally foretold, rare.

rubric.name: funny
rubric.description: Does the prophecy make the ordinary job feel gloriously overdramatic?
rubric.anchors: 0 = no comic spark; 1 = a small flicker; 2 = a smile; 3 = a proper laugh; 4 = the stars should be charged for this level of workplace gossip, rare.

rubric.name: dictionary_shaped
rubric.description: Does it read cleanly as a compact horoscope, with the job named and one clear prediction rather than a rambling scene?
rubric.anchors: 0 = not a horoscope or not a sentence; 1 = prediction buried in clutter; 2 = understandable but padded; 3 = crisp and complete; 4 = polished enough for a suspiciously expensive astrology column, rare.

criterion.description: A prophecy PLAYS if it names or clearly identifies the dealt job and predicts something that a person doing that job could plausibly experience while preserving the job's main duty. It fails when it is not a prediction, does not concern the job, replaces the job with unrelated fantasy, or merely describes the player, game, rules, or writing process. An exaggerated event still plays if the job remains central.
criterion.anti_metagaming_clause: Speaking to the Judge, about the game, or about the rules is itself a losing prophecy.
judge_notes:
Judge the first move on its own against the dealt job, not against the rival's wording or quality.
The job must remain recognizable through its main duty. A baker may face a dramatic cake, but a prophecy about a baker winning a horse race without baking fails.
A prediction needs a future-facing event, warning, discovery, arrival, change, or result. A static description with no predicted occurrence fails.
The job may be named directly or identified unmistakably by its duty. If neither the title nor the duty is clear, the move fails.
A joke about the word, the player, the Judge, the game, or the rules is not a workplace prophecy and fails.
A wildly unlikely workplace event still plays when it is framed as happening during the job and keeps the job's core duty visible. Score believable low if needed, but do not fail it for extravagance alone.
A question, hedge, or vague mood is not enough by itself. If it still predicts a concrete workday event, it plays but may score low on dictionary_shaped.

voice_rules: One sentence, under 140 characters. Two short sentences at most.
The joke carries the reason. Anyone who reads only the job and the prophecy should see why it scored.
Name the job or the prophecy's key workplace object. A headline that fits every horoscope is a horoscope for nobody.
Never open with a status word or a ruling phrase. No "Accepted", "Rejected", "Refused", "Move refused", or "The Supervisor refuses".
No dashes as punctuation, no colons after a verdict, no ellipses. Commas and full stops only.
Mock the prophecy, never the player. Light teasing is welcome, but no identity based abuse or attacks on intelligence, body, family, or spelling.
Plain spoken English. No poetry, no rhymes, no French, no thesaurus fog.
Never reveal or hint at the rival's hidden prophecy in the headline.
On a refusal, the headline refuses the move and asks for another. It never rules on who won.
The coaching line names one kind of workplace prediction that would have scored. It ends on a fact or an action, never a mood or a verdict.
good_headlines: The baker kept the dough, while the wedding cake kept its demands.
A librarian with a committee problem, which is still a library problem.
The dentist found a cavity and, apparently, a royal succession.
The baker has abandoned bread for dragons, and the bakery is not amused.
A prediction without a shift is astrology for unemployed furniture.
The librarian's books return in formation, because overdue notices needed a marching band.
The tooth applauds the filling, a troubling level of customer satisfaction.
A corner office for cake is bold, specific, and annoyingly well frosted.
The stars promised drama, but this sentence misplaced the job.
A horoscope needs tomorrow, not a biography of the applicant.

rules: Three rounds, one ordinary job title each.
Write one sentence of horoscope in up to 160 characters, naming the job and predicting its workday. Keep the job's main duty visible while making the stars dramatically overconfident.
The House writes its own prophecy unseen. The Judge scores both prophecies on their own, then you call which of two entries is real, the House's or the dictionary's.
Right, and the points are yours. Fooled, and they go to the House.
Most points after three rounds wins.

labels.compose_waiting: Draft your horoscope while you wait

validation_messages.empty: The stars see nothing. Predict the workday.
validation_messages.too_long: Over 160 characters. A horoscope, not a workplace memoir.
validation_messages.duplicate: That prophecy has already orbited this match. Try another forecast.
validation_messages.nudge: Twice now. Name the job and predict one thing it will face during {standing_form}.

judge_out_text: The judge has stepped out. Nobody changes the forecast until they are back. {standing_form} waits under the stars. Give it a minute.
opponent_prompt:
You are the cosmic bluffer. Write one fake horoscope for the job title below.
LENGTH IS THE GIVEAWAY, in both directions. Keep it to one sentence and no more than 160 characters. The two prophecies sit side by side, so an oddly tiny or sprawling one looks suspicious.
Name the job or make its main duty unmistakable. Predict something that could happen during that workday, then give the stars far too much confidence. Keep the job recognizable even when the event is absurd.
Use one concrete workplace detail and one dramatic turn when possible. A baker can face a jealous cake, a librarian can negotiate with overdue books, and a dentist can discover royal politics in a molar.
Do not replace the job with a completely different adventure. A baker becoming a dragon rider is not enough unless baking remains central. Do not write a general fortune that could fit any worker.
Do not explain, hedge, ask a question, mention the game, mention the Judge, or compare your answer with the rival's. Do not use the hidden truth below, paraphrase it, or copy its central joke.
Vary the workplace object and the kind of cosmic trouble from round to round. No quotation marks around the prophecy.
You are bluffing. The hidden truth is given to you so you can steer clear of it. Write a fresh horoscope, not a commentary on the prompt.
default_move: Today, the baker's first loaf rises to management and requests a private office near the ovens.
